claim: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated cellular giants formed by the fusion of mononuclear myoblasts.
source: Skeletal muscle fibers are multinucleated cellular giants formed by the fusion of mononuclear myoblasts.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in muscle biology presented in the abstract.

claim: Finger-like projections coincident with myoblast fusion have been implicated in the fusion process.
source: Several molecules involved in myoblast fusion have been discovered, and finger-like projections coincident with myoblast fusion have also been implicated in the fusion process.
evidence: This statement references prior observations about cellular projections during fusion.

claim: The cellular projections observed during myoblast fusion are filopodia generated by class X myosin (Myo10).
source: We demonstrate that these projections are filopodia generated by class X myosin (Myo10), an unconventional myosin motor protein specialized for filopodia.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Myo10 is highly expressed by differentiating myoblasts.
source: We further show that Myo10 is highly expressed by differentiating myoblasts, and Myo10 ablation inhibits both filopodia formation and myoblast fusion in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein and gene expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Myo10 ablation inhibits filopodia formation in myoblasts in vitro.
source: We further show that Myo10 is highly expressed by differentiating myoblasts, and Myo10 ablation inhibits both filopodia formation and myoblast fusion in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated through knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Myo10 ablation inhibits myoblast fusion in vitro.
source: We further show that Myo10 is highly expressed by differentiating myoblasts, and Myo10 ablation inhibits both filopodia formation and myoblast fusion in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fusion assays in Myo10 knockdown cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: Myo10 labels regenerating muscle fibers associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
source: In vivo, Myo10 labels regenerating muscle fibers associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and acute muscle injury.
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence of mdx mouse and DMD patient muscle sections in Figure 4.

claim: Myo10 labels regenerating muscle fibers associated with acute muscle injury.
source: In vivo, Myo10 labels regenerating muscle fibers associated with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and acute muscle injury.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cardiotoxin and glycerol injury models shown in Figure 4.

claim: Conditional loss of Myo10 from satellite cells severely impairs postnatal muscle regeneration in mice.
source: In mice, conditional loss of Myo10 from muscle-resident stem cells, known as satellite cells, severely impairs postnatal muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is demonstrated using Pax7Cre-ERT2 conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: Myomaker is detected in myoblast filopodia.
source: Furthermore, the muscle fusion proteins Myomaker and Myomixer are detected in myoblast filopodia.
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 5.

claim: Myomixer is detected in myoblast filopodia.
source: Furthermore, the muscle fusion proteins Myomaker and Myomixer are detected in myoblast filopodia.
evidence: This is shown through immunofluorescence in Figure 5.

claim: Myo10-driven filopodia facilitate multinucleated mammalian muscle formation.
source: These data demonstrate that Myo10-driven filopodia facilitate multinucleated mammalian muscle formation.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Satellite cells normally remain in a quiescent state positioned between the sarcolemma and basement membrane of muscle fibers.
source: In postnatal muscle, this fusion process is initiated by the activation of muscle-resident stem cells, known as satellite cells, which normally remain in a quiescent state positioned between the sarcolemma and basement membrane of muscle fibers (Mauro, 1961).
evidence: This is established knowledge about satellite cell biology, supported by citation.

claim: Following an activation stimulus, satellite cells give rise to myoblast progeny which proliferate, differentiate, and fuse to bring the muscle back to homeostasis.
source: Following an activation stimulus, satellite cells give rise to myoblast progeny which proliferate, differentiate, and fuse to bring the muscle back to homeostasis (Charge and Rudnicki, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about satellite cell function, supported by citation.

claim: The fusion of mammalian myoblasts requires the merging of two apposing lipid bilayers.
source: The fusion of mammalian myoblasts requires the merging of two apposing lipid bilayers and has been shown to involve several widely expressed protein classes, including cytoskeleton elements (Charrasse et al., 2006; Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018; Vasyutina et al., 2009), phagocytosis receptors (Hamoud et al., 2014; Hochreiter-Hufford et al., 2013; Park et al., 2016), and calcium-sensing membrane repair proteins (Leikina et al., 2013; Posey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about membrane fusion mechanics.

claim: Mammalian myoblast fusion involves cytoskeleton elements.
source: The fusion of mammalian myoblasts requires the merging of two apposing lipid bilayers and has been shown to involve several widely expressed protein classes, including cytoskeleton elements (Charrasse et al., 2006; Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018; Vasyutina et al., 2009), phagocytosis receptors (Hamoud et al., 2014; Hochreiter-Hufford et al., 2013; Park et al., 2016), and calcium-sensing membrane repair proteins (Leikina et al., 2013; Posey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mammalian myoblast fusion involves phagocytosis receptors.
source: The fusion of mammalian myoblasts requires the merging of two apposing lipid bilayers and has been shown to involve several widely expressed protein classes, including cytoskeleton elements (Charrasse et al., 2006; Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018; Vasyutina et al., 2009), phagocytosis receptors (Hamoud et al., 2014; Hochreiter-Hufford et al., 2013; Park et al., 2016), and calcium-sensing membrane repair proteins (Leikina et al., 2013; Posey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Mammalian myoblast fusion involves calcium-sensing membrane repair proteins.
source: The fusion of mammalian myoblasts requires the merging of two apposing lipid bilayers and has been shown to involve several widely expressed protein classes, including cytoskeleton elements (Charrasse et al., 2006; Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018; Vasyutina et al., 2009), phagocytosis receptors (Hamoud et al., 2014; Hochreiter-Hufford et al., 2013; Park et al., 2016), and calcium-sensing membrane repair proteins (Leikina et al., 2013; Posey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Myomaker has been identified as a membrane protein essential for myoblast fusion.
source: Myomaker (Millay et al., 2013) and Myomixer (aka Myomerger and Minion; the product of the Gm7325 gene; Bi et al., 2017; Quinn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017) have been identified as being membrane proteins essential for myoblast fusion.
evidence: This is established by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Myomixer has been identified as a membrane protein essential for myoblast fusion.
source: Myomaker (Millay et al., 2013) and Myomixer (aka Myomerger and Minion; the product of the Gm7325 gene; Bi et al., 2017; Quinn et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017) have been identified as being membrane proteins essential for myoblast fusion.
evidence: This is established by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Myomaker is required by both fusing cells.
source: Current evidence suggests that Myomaker is required by both fusing cells, while the requirement for Myomixer is only unilateral (Quinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The requirement for Myomixer is only unilateral.
source: Current evidence suggests that Myomaker is required by both fusing cells, while the requirement for Myomixer is only unilateral (Quinn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanisms regulating the function of Myomaker and Myomixer are currently unknown.
source: However, the mechanisms regulating the function of these proteins are currently unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Thin, actin-filled projections have been observed during the fusion of murine myoblasts.
source: Thin, actin-filled projections have been observed during the fusion of murine (Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018) and zebrafish (Gurevich et al., 2016) myoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Thin, actin-filled projections have been observed during the fusion of zebrafish myoblasts.
source: Thin, actin-filled projections have been observed during the fusion of murine (Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018) and zebrafish (Gurevich et al., 2016) myoblasts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Filopodia are thin, membrane-enclosed projections of actin bundles that are important for cellular behaviors such as path finding during migration, interaction with the extracellular matrix, and cell-to-cell communication.
source: These structures appear to be filopodia, which are thin, membrane-enclosed projections of actin bundles that are important for cellular behaviors such as path finding during migration, interaction with the extracellular matrix, and cell-to-cell communication (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about filopodia function, supported by citation.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is well established as an enactor of Drosophila myoblast fusion.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is well established as an enactor of Drosophila myoblast fusion (Abmayr and Pavlath, 2012; Chen, 2011), with filopodia suggested to be involved in this process (Segal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Filopodia have been suggested to be involved in Drosophila myoblast fusion.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is well established as an enactor of Drosophila myoblast fusion (Abmayr and Pavlath, 2012; Chen, 2011), with filopodia suggested to be involved in this process (Segal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: No members of the myosin superfamily of molecular motors have been reported to have a direct role in the muscle fusion process.
source: Despite actin cytoskeletal involvement in the fusion of both vertebrate and arthropod myoblasts, no members of the myosin superfamily of molecular motors have been reported to have a direct role in the muscle fusion process.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature prior to this study.

claim: Myosin superfamily members perform actin-associated functions in all cell types.
source: Myosin superfamily members perform actin-associated functions in all cell types.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myosin function.

claim: Eleven classes of unconventional myosins are expressed in mammals.
source: This includes the conventional (class II) myosins, such as those that power muscle contraction, and several classes of 'unconventional' myosins, of which 11 are expressed in mammals (Berg et al., 2001; Odronitz and Kollmar, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Class X myosin (Myo10) is an unconventional myosin involved in the formation and elongation of filopodia in mammalian cells.
source: Class X myosin (Myo10) is an unconventional myosin involved in the formation and elongation of filopodia in mammalian cells (Berg and Cheney, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Myo10 function, supported by citation.

claim: Myo10 consists of an N-terminal motor domain, a lever arm with three calmodulin-binding sites and a single alpha helical domain, and a C-terminal tail containing a pleckstrin homology (PH), a myosin tail homology 4 (MyTH4), and a 4.1/Ezrin/Radixin/Moesin (FERM) domain.
source: Myo10 consists of an N-terminal motor domain, a lever arm with three calmodulin-binding sites and a single alpha helical domain, and a C-terminal tail containing a pleckstrin homology (PH), a myosin tail homology 4 (MyTH4), and a 4.1/Ezrin/Radixin/Moesin (FERM) domain (Kerber and Cheney, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Myo10 structure, supported by citation.

claim: Upon activation, Myo10 forms an anti-parallel dimer that is optimized for the organization and movement along actin bundles.
source: Upon activation, Myo10 forms an anti-parallel dimer that is optimized for the organization and movement along actin bundles (Ropars et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Myo10 function, supported by citation.

claim: Myo10-driven filopodia are involved in processes such as neural and vascular development.
source: Myo10-driven filopodia are involved in processes such as neural and vascular development (Heimsath et al., 2017; Pi et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Undifferentiated myoblasts exhibit many thin cellular projections.
source: Undifferentiated myoblasts of the murine C2C12 cell line exhibit many thin cellular projections.
evidence: This is an observation from live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Thin cellular projections in undifferentiated myoblasts are actively elongating primarily at the leading edge of myoblasts.
source: Live imaging reveals that these projections are actively elongating primarily at the leading edge of myoblasts, while the trailing regions of the cells predominantly exhibit retraction fibers that become evident as the cells move (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C, Videos 1–2; summarized in Figure 1A), as commonly observed during cell migration (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: The trailing regions of undifferentiated myoblasts predominantly exhibit retraction fibers that become evident as the cells move.
source: Live imaging reveals that these projections are actively elongating primarily at the leading edge of myoblasts, while the trailing regions of the cells predominantly exhibit retraction fibers that become evident as the cells move (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C, Videos 1–2; summarized in Figure 1A), as commonly observed during cell migration (Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1 and supplementary figures.

claim: Upon induction of differentiation, myoblasts undergo morphological changes characterized by cellular elongation, loss of distinct directional polarity, and increased incidence of cellular projections from the entirety of the cell body.
source: Upon induction of differentiation by switching the cells to low-serum media conditions, myoblasts undergo morphological changes characterized by cellular elongation, loss of distinct directional polarity, and increased incidence of cellular projections from the entirety of the cell body (Video 3).
evidence: This is observed through live-cell imaging during differentiation.

claim: Differentiated myotubes display an array of dynamic and static projections at the lateral edges, prominent dorsal protrusions along the cell body, and arm-like lamellipodial extensions adorned with thin projections.
source: As the differentiation process proceeds to the formation of multinucleated myotubes, the cells display an array of dynamic and static projections at the lateral edges, prominent dorsal protrusions along the cell body, and arm-like lamellipodial extensions adorned with thin projections that can protrude from any part of the cell (Figure 1B and Videos 4–7; summarized in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging shown in Figure 1 and videos.

claim: The lengths of extending projections from myotubes are significantly longer than those from the leading edge of myoblasts.
source: The lengths of extending projections from myotubes are significantly longer than those from the leading edge of myoblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and scanning electron micrographs confirm that these dorsal projections from myotubes are of consistent structure and size of thin, actin-based cellular projections known as filopodia (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Scanning electron micrographs confirm that dorsal projections from myotubes are of consistent structure and size of thin, actin-based cellular projections known as filopodia.
source: The lengths of extending projections from myotubes are significantly longer than those from the leading edge of myoblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and scanning electron micrographs confirm that these dorsal projections from myotubes are of consistent structure and size of thin, actin-based cellular projections known as filopodia (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Live imaging of differentiating myoblast cultures reveals the involvement of cellular projections in muscle cell fusion.
source: Live imaging of differentiating myoblast cultures reveals the involvement of these structures in muscle cell fusion, as witnessed through fusion induced by projections extending from the lateral edge of myotubes (Figure 1E–F, Video 8), as well as by projection-laden lamellipodial extensions (Figure 1G, Videos 9–10).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging of fusion events shown in Figure 1 and videos.

claim: Myo10 protein content increases during the time course of myoblast differentiation.
source: Myo10 protein content (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and Myo10 gene expression (Figure 2B) increase during the time course of myoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunoblotting and gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Myo10 gene expression increases during the time course of myoblast differentiation.
source: Myo10 protein content (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and Myo10 gene expression (Figure 2B) increase during the time course of myoblast differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through real-time PCR analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Myo10 immunofluorescence localizes specifically to differentiated myotubes.
source: Myo10 immunofluorescence localizes specifically to differentiated myotubes (Figure 2C), which are confirmed to have expression of myosin heavy chain (MHC; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Myo10-positive projections observed on myotubes contain actin filaments (F-actin).
source: The Myo10-positive projections observed on these myotubes also contain actin filaments (F-actin; Figure 2E), a key feature of filopodia.
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-staining with phalloidin shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Insoluble Myo10 is found distinctly at the tips of F-actin bundles in differentiating myoblasts.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) of insoluble myotube cellular remnants following soluble fraction extraction reveals that insoluble Myo10 is associated with the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and can be distinctly visualized at the tips of actin bundles that appear to be within myotube filopodia (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The full-length Myo10 promoter contains 14 consensus E-Box motifs (CANNTG).
source: In agreement with Myo10 expression becoming highly activated in myoblasts during myogenic differentiation, analysis of the full-length Myo10 promoter (Lai et al., 2013) revealed the presence of 14 consensus E-Box motifs (CANNTG; depicted in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the Myo10 promoter sequence.

claim: E-Box motifs are DNA elements bound by myogenic regulator factors (MRFs), such as MyoD and Myogenin, during myogenesis.
source: These motifs are DNA elements bound by myogenic regulator factors (MRFs), such as MyoD and Myogenin, during myogenesis (Tapscott, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MRF function, supported by citation.

claim: Activation of the Myo10 promoter increases proportionally with Myo10 content as myoblast differentiation progresses.
source: Activation of the Myo10 promoter, as determined by the RFP/GFP-CAAX ratio in immunoblots, is confirmed to increase proportionally with Myo10 content as myoblast differentiation progresses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through reporter assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Myo10-positive mononuclear myocytes exhibit positive staining for both MyoD and Myogenin during the first day of differentiation.
source: Consistent with MRF-mediated activation of Myo10 during myoblast differentiation, Myo10-positive mononuclear myocytes exhibit positive staining for both MyoD and Myogenin, which have both been shown to bind to the Myo10 promoter (Cao et al., 2006), during the first day of differentiation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2G.

claim: MyoD and Myogenin have both been shown to bind to the Myo10 promoter.
source: Consistent with MRF-mediated activation of Myo10 during myoblast differentiation, Myo10-positive mononuclear myocytes exhibit positive staining for both MyoD and Myogenin, which have both been shown to bind to the Myo10 promoter (Cao et al., 2006), during the first day of differentiation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is established by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Myo10 knockdown results in efficient loss of Myo10 gene expression during both growth and differentiation culture conditions.
source: Myo10 KD results in efficient loss of Myo10 gene expression during both growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) and differentiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) culture conditions, as well as reduction of Myo10 protein from both culture conditions (Figure 3A) and loss of Myo10 IF during differentiation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through gene expression and protein analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Myogenic differentiation potential per se is not affected by loss of Myo10.
source: Myogenic differentiation potential per se is not affected by loss of Myo10, as MHC protein and Myh2 gene expression do not differ between control and Myo10 KD lines after 5 days of differentiation (Figure 3A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of differentiation markers shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Loss of Myo10 has a significant effect on prevalence of cellular projections.
source: Loss of Myo10 does, however, have a significant effect on prevalence of cellular projections, which are therefore filopodia, as Myo10 KD myocytes exhibit less dorsal protrusions (Figure 3C) and no detectable extending filopodia (Figure 3D; Video 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated through imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3.

claim: Myo10 KD myocytes exhibit no detectable extending filopodia.
source: Loss of Myo10 does, however, have a significant effect on prevalence of cellular projections, which are therefore filopodia, as Myo10 KD myocytes exhibit less dorsal protrusions (Figure 3C) and no detectable extending filopodia (Figure 3D; Video 12).
evidence: This is demonstrated through live-cell imaging shown in Figure 3D and Video 12.

claim: The primary cellular protrusions displayed by Myo10 KD cells appear as blebs reaching to the cell periphery in order to create connections to the surface substrate.
source: The primary cellular protrusions displayed by Myo10 KD cells appear as blebs reaching to the cell periphery in order to create connections to the surface substrate (Video 13), which are significantly shorter in length when compared to the thin and distinct Myo10-driven filopodia of control shRNA myocytes (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is observed through live-cell imaging shown in Video 13 and quantified in Figure 3.

claim: Loss of Myo10 does not prevent the formation of lamellipodial extensions.
source: Loss of Myo10 does not prevent the formation of lamellipodial extensions; however, they are devoid of detectable thin projections, which are thus confirmed to be filopodia (Video 13).
evidence: This is observed through live-cell imaging shown in Video 13.

claim: Loss of Myo10 nearly abolishes multinucleated myotube formation following 7 days of differentiation.
source: The involvement of filopodia in myoblast fusion is also confirmed, as loss of Myo10 nearly abolishes multinucleated myotube formation following 7 days of differentiation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through fusion assays shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Loss of myoblast fusion in Myo10 KD cells can be partially rescued by expression of exogenous Myo10.
source: This can be partially rescued by expression of exogenous Myo10, using an N-terminal mApple tagged human Myo10 construct (RFP-Myo10; Figure 3G–H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), as determined by the quantification of MHC-positive myocytes containing three or more nuclei following 7 days of differentiation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through rescue experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The rescue of Myo10 KD myoblast fusion by exogenous Myo10 expression requires Myo10's cargo-binding functions.
source: The rescue of Myo10 KD myoblast fusion by exogenous Myo10 expression is not attributed to solely filopodia formation, but requires Myo10's cargo-binding functions, as a truncated RFP-Myo10 construct lacking the C-terminal PH, MyTH4, and FERM domains (RFP-Myo10ΔCBD) does not restore myoblast fusion despite promoting similar numbers of filopodia of only slightly reduced lengths (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with truncated Myo10 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The requirement of myoblast Myo10 for fusogenic activity appears to be a requirement of both fusing cells.
source: Furthermore, the requirement of myoblast Myo10 for fusogenic activity appears to be a requirement of both fusing cells, as a mixture of control and Myo10 KD myoblasts having distinct fluorescent labels rarely results in the fusion of the two populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mixing experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Strong Myo10 immunoreactivity occurs within small muscle fibers of regenerating areas in mdx mouse muscle sections.
source: Strong Myo10 immunoreactivity within small muscle fibers of regenerating areas, which are identified by the presence of centrally located nuclei (Coulton et al., 1988), occurs in these muscle sections, with negligible signal detection in regions of stable muscle fibers (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of mdx muscle shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DMD patient biopsy samples contain many small, Myo10-positive fibers localized to regenerating foci.
source: This Myo10 expression pattern is also observed in human muscle, as DMD patient biopsy samples contain many small, Myo10-positive fibers localized to regenerating foci (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of DMD patient samples shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Myo10 is expressed in muscle during times that are expected to have high amounts of myoblast fusion, including muscle regeneration.
source: Thus, Myo10 is expressed in muscle during times that are expected to have high amounts of myoblast fusion, including muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Myo10 in regenerating muscle.

claim: Myo10 is an effective marker to label regenerating skeletal muscle fibers in vivo.
source: These data also demonstrate that Myo10 is an effective marker to label regenerating skeletal muscle fibers in vivo, which may be a useful tool to identify newly formed muscle fibers in lieu of developmental MHC isoforms.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific expression pattern of Myo10 in regenerating muscle.

claim: Tamoxifen-induced Cre expression results in efficient ablation of Myo10-positive muscle fibers in Pax7-M10cKO mice 4 days following CTX injection.
source: Tamoxifen-induced Cre expression (via the protocol depicted in Figure 4D) results in efficient ablation of Myo10-positive muscle fibers (Figure 4E) and Myo10 protein content (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) in Pax7-M10cKO mice 4 days following CTX injection.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence and immunoblotting shown in Figure 4.

claim: At 8 days following CTX injection, Pax7-M10cKO muscles exhibit impaired regeneration compared to Pax7-WT muscles.
source: At 8 days following CTX injection, Pax7-WT muscles demonstrate robust regeneration, while Pax7-M10cKO muscles exhibit impaired regeneration, as evidenced by fewer and smaller myocytes present in regenerating musculature (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated through histological analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pax7-M10cKO muscle regenerative defects are exhibited following freeze injury.
source: Pax7-M10cKO muscle regenerative defects are also exhibited following freeze injury, a more severe muscle injury model (Hardy et al., 2016), of which affected Myo10-deficient musculature is largely replaced by intramuscular fibrosis following 21 days of recovery (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through freeze injury experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myo10 is important for regenerative myogenesis.
source: Thus, Myo10 is important for regenerative myogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the impaired regeneration observed in Myo10-deficient mice.

claim: Mononuclear myocytes early in the differentiation process exhibit strong extracellular staining of Myomixer on most of the cell periphery, including cellular projections.
source: Mononuclear myocytes early in the differentiation process exhibit strong extracellular staining of Myomixer on most of the cell periphery, including cellular projections (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In mononuclear myocytes early in differentiation, Myomaker is localized primarily to vesicular structures that are particularly evident in the perinuclear cap region.
source: In these cells, Myomaker is localized primarily to vesicular structures that are particularly evident in the perinuclear cap region (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The perinuclear localization of Myomaker agrees with the previously reported Golgi localization of Myomaker.
source: This agrees with the previously reported Golgi localization of Myomaker (Gamage et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: In multinucleated myotubes, Myomixer remains prominently localized at the cellular periphery.
source: In multinucleated myotubes, Myomixer remains prominently localized at the cellular periphery, while Myomaker is additionally observed in puncta found in close proximity to the cell membrane along the cell body and cellular projections, including filopodia protruding from lamellipodial extensions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5.

claim: In multinucleated myotubes, Myomaker is observed in puncta found in close proximity to the cell membrane along the cell body and cellular projections, including filopodia protruding from lamellipodial extensions.
source: In multinucleated myotubes, Myomixer remains prominently localized at the cellular periphery, while Myomaker is additionally observed in puncta found in close proximity to the cell membrane along the cell body and cellular projections, including filopodia protruding from lamellipodial extensions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5.

claim: Myo10-positive cells co-expressing Myomaker and Myomixer are observed during the first day of differentiation.
source: Myo10-positive cells co-expressing Myomaker and Myomixer are observed during the first day of differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), indicating temporal regulation of these myogenic genes are synchronized.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The expression of Myomixer and Myomaker are not dependent on Myo10.
source: The expression of Myomixer and Myomaker are not, however, dependent on Myo10, as both proteins are found in differentiated Myo10 KD myoblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of Myo10 KD cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In fully differentiated Myo10-positive myotubes, puncta of both Myomaker and Myomixer are observed in Myo10-filled filopodia.
source: In fully differentiated Myo10-positive myotubes, puncta of both Myomaker and Myomixer are observed in Myo10-filled filopodia (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence shown in Figure 5.

claim: Myomaker and Myomixer co-localize with Myo10 puncta in the filopodia remnants of insoluble myotube fractions.
source: Furthermore, these proteins are found to co-localize with Myo10 puncta in the filopodia remnants of insoluble myotube fractions (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of insoluble fractions shown in Figure 5.

claim: The localization of both Myomaker and Myomixer to Myo10-positive filopodia is observed when functional Flag-tagged versions of these proteins are exogenously expressed in differentiating myoblast cultures.
source: The localization of both Myomaker and Myomixer to Myo10-positive filopodia is also observed when functional Flag-tagged versions of these proteins, namely the Myomaker-F203 (Millay et al., 2013) and Myomixer-Flag (Zhang et al., 2017) constructs, are exogenously expressed in differentiating myoblast cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments with Flag-tagged constructs shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sections from regenerating Pax7-WT muscle display Myo10-labeled filopodia decorated with Myomixer puncta.
source: Sections from regenerating Pax7-WT muscle also display Myo10-labeled filopodia decorated with Myomixer puncta (Figure 5E), suggesting this relationship also exists in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of regenerating muscle shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Myomaker- and Myomixer-positive cells of regenerating Pax7-M10cKO muscle do not have cellular projections.
source: Such cellular projections are not found on Myomaker- and Myomixer-positive cells of regenerating Pax7-M10cKO muscle (Figure 5F), which exhibit thin morphologies similar to Myo10 KD myoblasts rather than robust myotube formation found in wild-type muscle sections (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence of Pax7-M10cKO muscle shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Muscle filopodia provide a means to enable cellular connections that facilitate the function of fusion proteins upon delivery to a cellular target.
source: These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that muscle filopodia provide a means to enable cellular connections that facilitate the function of these fusion proteins upon delivery to a cellular target.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the localization data.

claim: No motor proteins have been previously described to have a direct role in the myoblast fusion process itself.
source: While the involvement of the actin cytoskeleton is well documented in both arthropod and mammalian myoblast fusion (Chen, 2011; Millay et al., 2013; Peckham, 2008; Randrianarison-Huetz et al., 2018; Segal et al., 2016), no motor proteins have been previously described to have a direct role in the fusion process itself.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature prior to this study.

claim: Non-muscle myosin II has been implicated in myoblast fusion, serving as a sub-sarcolemmal mechanosensor.
source: Only the conventional myosin, non-muscle myosin II, has been implicated in myoblast fusion, serving as a sub-sarcolemmal mechanosensor (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: This report provides the first described role of Myo10 in mammalian muscle.
source: The current report also provides the first described role of Myo10 in mammalian muscle, which has only been previously detected in muscle via dystrophic muscle gene expression arrays (Marotta et al., 2009) and Myo10 promoter binding by the muscle regulatory factors MyoD and Myogenin (Cao et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement claims novelty of the findings.

claim: A myosin motor involved in myoblast fusion has not been identified in Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, a myosin motor involved in myoblast fusion has not been identified in Drosophila, which lack Myo10.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in Drosophila research.

claim: It is likely that another member of MyTH4-FERM containing myosins, such as the class XV myosin (Myo15) homolog Sisyphus, is adapted for the role of filopodia formation in insect muscle.
source: It is likely that another member of MyTH4-FERM containing myosins, such as the class XV myosin (Myo15) homolog Sisyphus (Liu et al., 2008), is adapted for the role of filopodia formation in insect muscle.
evidence: This is speculation based on structural similarities between myosin classes.

claim: Loss of Myo15 in Drosophila substantially reduces larva viability and causes abnormal neuromuscular junction formation.
source: A recent study has demonstrated that loss of Myo15 in Drosophila substantially reduces larva viability and causes abnormal neuromuscular junction formation, whereas muscle-specific Myo15 overexpression causes the development of peculiar F-actin structures in myocytes (Rich et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The premise of filopodia-facilitated myoblast fusion appears to be a convergent evolutionary feature of multinucleated muscle formation.
source: While the definitive identification of a myosin motor that drives insect muscle filopodia awaits further investigation, the premise of filopodia-facilitated myoblast fusion appears to be a convergent evolutionary feature of multinucleated muscle formation (Segal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations across species.

claim: The physical presentation of molecules at a distance from the cell body via cytoskeletal extensions is an important aspect of skeletal muscle development.
source: Thus, the physical presentation of molecules at a distance from the cell body via cytoskeletal extensions is an important aspect of skeletal muscle development as it is in the development of other tissue types (Pi et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings and comparison to other systems.

claim: A patient having two alleles for a truncating MYO10 mutation has been recently identified.
source: These data are potentially of clinical significance, as a patient having two alleles for a truncating MYO10 mutation has been recently identified (Patel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on a clinical case report cited in the manuscript.

claim: It is possible that an underlying myopathy may exist or develop in the MYO10-deficient patient as a result of impairments in muscle recovery from injury.
source: While this individual was found on basis of having microphthalmia, a developmental eye defect, it is possible that an underlying myopathy may exist or develop as a result of impairments in muscle recovery from injury.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in mice.

claim: Microphthalmia is associated with several syndromes that also present with myopathy or neuromuscular disorders, including Walker-Walburg syndrome and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
source: In fact, microphthalmia is also associated with several syndromes that also present with myopathy or neuromuscular disorders, including Walker-Walburg syndrome (Vajsar and Schachter, 2006) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (Fernandez-Torre et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several MYO10 single-nucleotide polymorphisms have been identified.
source: Furthermore, several MYO10 single-nucleotide polymorphisms have been identified (Burghardt et al., 2010), including missense mutations in the N-terminal motor domain.
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Individuals harboring MYO10 missense mutations in the motor domain may exhibit muscle regenerative defects.
source: Mutations such as these have the potential to create dominant-negative Myo10 molecules if motor function is impaired or destroyed, and individuals harboring such polymorphisms may exhibit muscle regenerative defects, as demonstrated by loss of Myo10 in mice.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in mice and knowledge of dominant-negative effects.

claim: The identification of a Myo10-deficient patient confirms findings in mice that loss of Myo10 is not absolutely lethal.
source: The identification of a Myo10-deficient patient also confirms findings in mice that loss of Myo10 is not absolutely lethal, although less than half of Myo10-null mice survive birth, and those that do survive exhibit developmental deficits (Heimsath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on comparison of human and mouse data.

claim: Less than half of Myo10-null mice survive birth.
source: The identification of a Myo10-deficient patient also confirms findings in mice that loss of Myo10 is not absolutely lethal, although less than half of Myo10-null mice survive birth, and those that do survive exhibit developmental deficits (Heimsath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Myo10-null mice that survive birth exhibit developmental deficits.
source: The identification of a Myo10-deficient patient also confirms findings in mice that loss of Myo10 is not absolutely lethal, although less than half of Myo10-null mice survive birth, and those that do survive exhibit developmental deficits (Heimsath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Decreased Myo10-null embryonic survivability indicates that Myo10-driven filopodia serve to increase the probability of proper cellular connectivity during developmental processes.
source: These evidences of decreased Myo10-null embryonic survivability further indicate that Myo10-driven filopodia serve to increase the probability of proper cellular connectivity during developmental processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the survival data.

claim: The surviving Myo10-null animals have fused muscle fibers.
source: The fact that the surviving Myo10-null animals have fused muscle fibers likely indicates that myoblasts are in close opposition during development, lessening the dependence on distal interactions mediated by filopodia.
evidence: This is an observation about Myo10-null mice.

claim: Myoblasts are in close opposition during development, lessening the dependence on distal interactions mediated by filopodia.
source: The fact that the surviving Myo10-null animals have fused muscle fibers likely indicates that myoblasts are in close opposition during development, lessening the dependence on distal interactions mediated by filopodia.
evidence: This is an inference to explain why Myo10-null mice can have fused muscle.

claim: Satellite cell-derived myoblasts of injured adult muscles must traverse much larger distances in order to locate and fuse with each other, creating a greater dependence on filopodia for postnatal muscle repair than for embryonic muscle development.
source: In contrast, satellite cell-derived myoblasts of injured adult muscles must traverse much larger distances in order to locate and fuse with each other, creating a greater dependence on filopodia for postnatal muscle repair than for embryonic muscle development.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference between developmental and regenerative myogenesis.

claim: It is currently hypothesized that Myomaker's role in cellular fusion is the promotion of outer membrane leaflet mixing (i.e. hemifusion) between cells.
source: It is currently hypothesized that Myomaker's role in cellular fusion is the promotion of outer membrane leaflet mixing (i.e. hemifusion) between cells, while Myomixer acts as an inducer of intercellular pore formation by promoting positive spontaneous membrane curvature within hemifusion structures (Golani et al., 2021; Leikina et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on current hypotheses in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Myomixer acts as an inducer of intercellular pore formation by promoting positive spontaneous membrane curvature within hemifusion structures.
source: It is currently hypothesized that Myomaker's role in cellular fusion is the promotion of outer membrane leaflet mixing (i.e. hemifusion) between cells, while Myomixer acts as an inducer of intercellular pore formation by promoting positive spontaneous membrane curvature within hemifusion structures (Golani et al., 2021; Leikina et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on current hypotheses in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The actions of Myomaker and Myomixer are consistent with the concept of their delivery by Myo10-driven filopodia in order to create an intermediate structure that is essentially a tunneling nanotube.
source: These actions are consistent with the concept of their delivery by Myo10-driven filopodia in order to create an intermediate structure that is essentially a tunneling nanotube, whether configured as individual or bundled lumens (Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019), that precedes development of a full syncytium.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of fusion based on the localization data.

claim: Myo10-dependent formation of tunneling nanotubes has been suggested as a requirement for osteoclast differentiation into multinucleated cells.
source: Such a structural organization is suggested by the images provided in Figure 1F, and Myo10-dependent formation of tunneling nanotubes has been suggested as a requirement for osteoclast differentiation into multinucleated cells (Tasca et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on prior research in osteoclasts, cited in the manuscript.

claim: The failure of a C-terminal Myo10 truncation (RFP-Myo10ΔCBD) to restore myoblast fusogenic activity suggests Myo10 does have an active cargo-binding role in promoting fusion of mammalian myoblasts.
source: While it remains to be confirmed if Myo10 plays an active role in the localization and/or activity of these fusogenic proteins or whether Myo10-driven filopodia increase the probability proper cellular connectivity via increased surface area, the failure of a C-terminal Myo10 truncation (RFP-Myo10ΔCBD) to restore myoblast fusogenic activity, despite promoting filopodia formation, suggests Myo10 does have an active cargo-binding role in promoting fusion of mammalian myoblasts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the truncation experiments.

claim: The apparent requirement of Myo10 by both fusing cells suggests that Myomaker fusogenic activity may depend on filopodia driven by full-length (cargo-binding competent) Myo10.
source: Furthermore, the apparent requirement of Myo10 by both fusing cells, a feature also exhibited by Myomaker (Quinn et al., 2017), suggests that Myomaker fusogenic activity may depend on filopodia driven by full-length (cargo-binding competent) Myo10.
evidence: This is speculation based on the bilateral requirement of Myo10 and comparison to Myomaker.

claim: These data emphasize the importance of filopodia in the intricate biological processes required for proper development of higher-order organisms.
source: The findings detailed in this report describe a role of filopodia driven by the unconventional myosin, Myo10, in the formation of multinucleated skeletal muscle. These data further emphasize the importance of these fine cellular projections in the intricate biological processes required for proper development of higher-order organisms, and that perturbations to their formation and function have the ability to cause muscle pathology and potentially modify the course of muscle disease.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Perturbations to filopodia formation and function have the ability to cause muscle pathology and potentially modify the course of muscle disease.
source: The findings detailed in this report describe a role of filopodia driven by the unconventional myosin, Myo10, in the formation of multinucleated skeletal muscle. These data further emphasize the importance of these fine cellular projections in the intricate biological processes required for proper development of higher-order organisms, and that perturbations to their formation and function have the ability to cause muscle pathology and potentially modify the course of muscle disease.
evidence: This is speculation about clinical implications based on the findings.
